newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Sweden's Wallenbergs prepare for next generation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sweden's Wallenbergs prepare for next generation.

text.p: Sweden's most powerful family, the Wallenbergs, is preparing for the fifth generation to take the helm despite criticism that the dynasty is becoming too strong.

Peter Wallenberg, the 70-year-old head of the family, is taking a step back from the frontline of its extensive business empire, opening the way for either his son Jacob or nephew Marcus, both aged 41, to be eased into his shoes.
"It's really not yet clear who will head the family but the ground is being laid for a generation change," said David Bartal, author of a biography on the Wallenbergs.
Swedish business stalwart, Pehr Gyllenhammar, former head of AB Volvo, said the family's grip on Sweden continues to tighten even as the younger Wallenbergs prepare to take over,

He said it was not just the size of the Wallenberg holdings that created such power but its voting rights and the movement of business leaders seen as in the Wallenberg camp into non-family companies, giving the Wallenbergs a presence in half Sweden's top 30 companies.
"Sweden is today almost unique in how we have one single rich, monopoly of concentrated power," Gyllenhammar said in a television interview last week.
"In the longterm it's not healthy. Sweden needs more alternatives."
THE DYNASTY

The Wallenberg dynasty began in 1856 when Andre Oscar Wallenberg formed Stockholm's Enskilda Bank, now S-E-Banken, and became a shareholder in a number of industrial companies through investments and as collateral for its loans.
His sons Marcus and Knut continued to expand the business empire as did third generation brothers Marcus and Jacob.

The wheels of change started to turn again in the empire this month with fourth generation Peter Wallenberg announcing he was stepping down as chairman of Investor AB, the family's vast holding company set up in 1916.
Turning 71 this year, the family patriach decided it was time to hand over the baton. He said his move should be seen as a natural process and a generation change.

"I have seen this as a business decision. We needed to have new ideas at Investor, more than anything to lead the company towards more overseas investments," Wallenberg told a news conference after announcing he would step down at the annual meeting on April 14.
SURPRISE SUCCESSOR

But in a move that surprised the market, leading Swedish businessman Percy Barnevik, 56, was named as Wallenberg's successor -- the first time Investor has been run by a non-family member -- as the fifth generation is not yet ready.
"There will be time for the young people," Wallenberg said in a newspaper interview.
Barnevik is seen as a Wallenberg man, having sat on the Investor board since 1992 and chairman of international engineer ABB of which the Wallenbergs own a stake.
"Barnevik's such a strong figure he'll be more than just an interim administrator. He'll take initiatives," Bartal said.
INVESTOR PORTFOLIO

Investor is the hub of the Wallenberg empire -- and the largest single owner of shares on the Stockholm stock exchange with a portfolio worth 68 billion crowns ($9 billion) at the end of 1996 when the total bourse was worth 1,595 billion crowns.
The portfolio reads like a Swedish business directory -- with its voting rights controlling about a third of the bourse.
Investor holds 45 percent of voting rights in appliance maker AB Electrolux, 45 percent of truck group Scania and 36 percent in holding company Incentive AB.
It owns 50 percent of luxury car maker Saab.

Investor also has key voting rights in Sweden's two biggest companies, controlling 22 percent of telecoms Ericsson and three percent of capital and 12 percent of drugs company Astra with 10 percent of its capital.

Four years ago Investor hit a rocky patch with debts of $1 billion but a restructuring drive has turned the company around. With a cash pile of about 10 billion crowns at the end of 1996, it is starting to eye overseas opportunities.
Gyllenhammar said this concentration of power in Sweden was not good as there was no counterbalance.

"When a force is rich, really big and so strong it is natural that people think it is dangerous to say anything against it," said Gyllenhammar, now a merchant banker, who has always remained outside the Wallenberg camp.
Leif Johansson, former managing director of Electrolux, is now taking over as chief executive at Volvo, one of the major Swedish companies that is not Wallenberg run.
Volvo's managing director Soren Gyll is taking over as chairman at tool and engineer SKF, which is 12 percent owned by Investor, while Lars Thunell, head of insurer Trygg-Hansa is joining Astra.
Even Sweden's richest man, Stefan Persson, head of Swedish fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz, is involved with the Wallenbergs, sitting on the board of Electrolux.
"Even from the Wallenbergs' point of view it would be good for Volvo to remain strong and independent so that it can drive an alternative debate," Gyllenhammar said.
BANK ALSO A FOCAL POINT
While Investor shadows the other Wallenberg companies, the family's 18 percent holding of S-E-Banken also remains a focal point of the family's empire.

After years of preparation, Peter Wallenberg's eldest son, Jacob, is to become chief executive at S-E-Banken, replacing Bjorn Svedberg, Ericsson's chairman, who is joining Incentive's board. Jacob has worked at the bank since 1984.
Earlier this year S-E-Banken's merger talks with state-controlled Nordbanken collapsed but market players speculate that they could resume under the new leadership.
Investor chief executive Claes Dahlback, a key figure in the Wallenberg world, will also take a seat on the S-E-Banken baord this year with suggestions that he will be chairman next year.
Meanwhile Marcus, the son of Peter's brother Marc -- who committed suicide in 1971 -- is Investor's vice chief executive.
If Dahlback moves to chair S-E-Banken, this leaves the seat empty for Marcus to take over as chief executive.
"The analysis is correct," Peter Wallenberg told reporters when presented with this scenario.
With these moves completed, the Wallenberg empire will be firmly in the hands of the family's fifth generation although the new family head is yet to be made clear.
"But with Barnevik in charge, it could be another 10 to 15 years down the road before either Marcus or Jacob take over," said Bartal. ($ = 7.590 Swedish Crowns)
